speaker: Doctor
text: I need to ask if you experience any warning sensations or changes in awareness right before these episodes of unresponsiveness. Are they typically very brief, lasting only seconds, or do they last longer than a minute?

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes lasting 3–4 minutes each of facial grimacing and staring over the past month. During these episodes, he is nonresponsive and does not recall them afterward. He reports a muddy taste in his mouth before the onset of these episodes. His brother witnessed him waking up, staring, and making hand gestures during one episode. The patient felt lethargic and confused afterwards.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for those details; the "muddy taste" and hand gestures are significant clues. Given the duration of 3–4 minutes and the post-ictal confusion, this sounds more like a focal seizure than a typical absence seizure. Did you notice any specific body movements, like jerking or turning of the head, during these episodes?

REQUEST TEST: EEG (Electroencephalogram)
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Brain

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Electroencephalogram: Interictal spikes and sharp waves localized to the temporal lobes, more prominent on the right side. MRI_Brain: No evidence of mass lesions, infarctions, or structural abnormalities.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant previous medical history. No prior seizures or neurological evaluations. Social history: Enrolled in second grade. Lives with parents and one sibling. No reported use of medications or exposure to toxins.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies fever, headache, visual or auditory disturbances, weakness, or other systemic symptoms. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That previous diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis is highly unlikely given the patient's age and the specific semiology of staring, grimacing, and a "muddy taste," which are classic signs of temporal lobe epilepsy. Have there been any triggers like flashing lights or fatigue, and does he have a family history of seizures? REQUEST TEST: EEG (Electroencephalogram) focused on temporal lobe; REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Brain with contrast.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Electroencephalogram: Interictal spikes and sharp waves localized to the temporal lobes, more prominent on the right side. MRI_Brain: No evidence of mass lesions, infarctions, or structural abnormalities.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The EEG findings of interictal spikes localized to the right temporal lobe, combined with your history of ictal automatisms (hand gestures) and post-ictal confusion, strongly confirm a diagnosis of epilepsy. Given the specific lateralization and semiology, do you have a history of head trauma or any known brain infection in early childhood?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Right Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (Mesial Temporal Sclerosis)
